title: Watermelon for a Hangover: Does It Help? Citrulline Claims, Explained
excerpt: Is watermelon good for a hangover? What its water and sugar can do, why the citrulline detox claim is a stretch, the best ways to eat it, and who should go easy.
metaDescription: Is watermelon good for a hangover? What it really helps with, why the citrulline detox claim is a stretch, watermelon juice tips, and who should go easy.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** watermelon is a good thing to eat when you're hungover, mostly because it's about 92% water, it's easy on a queasy stomach, and it gives you a little natural sugar when your energy is flat. It is not a cure. The claim you'll see online, that the citrulline in watermelon "detoxes" alcohol or flushes your liver, goes well beyond the evidence. There is no good evidence that watermelon, watermelon juice, or citrulline makes your body clear alcohol or its toxic by-product faster, or that it measurably shortens a hangover. This guide explains what watermelon can and can't do, what the citrulline research actually says, whether to eat it before or after drinking, and who should go easy on it.

**The quick rules:** If watermelon sounds good, eat it. A cup or two of chilled cubes is a pleasant way to get fluid into you when plain water feels like a chore. Pair it with a real meal that has some protein, fat, and salt, because watermelon alone is light on all three. Don't count on it to fix a headache or brain fog. If you've been vomiting or had diarrhea, use an oral rehydration drink as well, since watermelon contains very little sodium. And if your stomach is sensitive to fruit sugars, a big bowl of watermelon can make bloating or loose stools worse, not better.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover from a night out should be clearly improving by the afternoon or evening and gone within about a day. **Get medical help if** you can't keep fluids down for many hours, you're vomiting repeatedly or see blood, you feel faint or very dizzy when you stand, you're barely peeing or your urine is very dark, your heart is pounding or skipping in a way that doesn't settle, or you're confused or hard to wake. Shaking, sweating, and anxiety that start a day or two after stopping drinking can be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover, and that needs a doctor, not a home remedy. If someone has signs of alcohol poisoning (slow or irregular breathing, cold or bluish skin, seizures, can't be woken), call 911.

## Is Watermelon Good for a Hangover? The Short, Honest Version

Yes, as food and as a source of fluid. No, as a treatment.

To see why, it helps to know what a hangover actually is. Researchers still don't agree on a single cause, but the main contributors are thought to be the immune system's inflammatory response to alcohol, poor-quality sleep, the toxic effects of acetaldehyde (the compound your liver makes when it breaks alcohol down), irritation of the stomach lining, swings in blood sugar, and a degree of fluid loss. Dehydration is part of the picture, but studies of hungover people have generally found that hydration markers and electrolyte levels don't line up very closely with how bad people feel. That's why drinking a lot of water helps you feel less parched but rarely makes a hangover disappear. Our guide on [whether water helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-water-help-a-hangover) goes into that in more detail.

Watermelon touches only a couple of those causes:

- **Fluid.** It's mostly water, so eating it counts toward rehydrating.
- **A little sugar.** It has some easy carbohydrate, which can help if you drank a lot and ate little.
- **An easy food.** It's cold, mild, and wet, which makes it one of the few things many people can stomach first thing.

It does nothing meaningful for inflammation, sleep loss, or acetaldehyde, which are the parts of a hangover that make you feel poisoned. No study we know of has tested watermelon as a hangover remedy in people. So treat it as a pleasant, sensible snack in a recovery morning, not as the thing that fixes it.

## What's Actually in Watermelon

Here is roughly what you get from one cup of diced watermelon (about 150 grams), based on standard nutrition databases such as the USDA's FoodData Central. Values vary a little with ripeness and variety.

| Nutrient | About per cup (150 g) | What it means for a hangover |
|---|---|---|
| Water | About 140 g (roughly 92%) | Real fluid, comparable to a small glass of water |
| Calories | About 45 | Very light, so it won't replace a meal |
| Sugar | About 9 g | A modest dose of quick energy, mostly fructose |
| Potassium | About 170 mg | Small, about a third of a banana |
| Sodium | Almost none (1 to 2 mg) | Not useful for replacing salt lost to vomiting or sweat |
| Vitamin C | About 12 mg | A minor contribution |
| Lycopene | A good source | An antioxidant pigment, but no evidence it eases hangovers |
| L-citrulline | A rich food source | The amino acid behind most of the online claims |

A few things stand out. Watermelon is excellent for fluid and pretty modest on everything else. The sodium figure matters most: when you've lost fluid by vomiting, sweating heavily, or having diarrhea, you lose sodium too, and watermelon won't put it back. That's the main reason it works better alongside salty food or a proper electrolyte drink than on its own.

## The Citrulline Claim: What the Research Really Says

Most "watermelon cures hangovers" articles hang on one ingredient: **L-citrulline**. Watermelon is one of the richest natural food sources of it (the name comes from *Citrullus*, the plant's scientific name), and the pale rind holds a good share of it. The claim usually goes something like this: citrulline helps your liver get rid of ammonia, so it helps "detox" alcohol, so it cures your hangover. Each step in that chain is weaker than the one before.

### What citrulline does in the body

Citrulline is an amino acid your body also makes on its own. Two of its jobs are relevant here:

1. **The urea cycle.** Your liver uses citrulline as one step in turning ammonia (a waste product from breaking down protein) into urea, which you then pee out. This is where the "detox" idea comes from.
2. **Nitric oxide.** Your kidneys convert citrulline into another amino acid, arginine, which your blood vessels use to make nitric oxide. Nitric oxide relaxes and widens blood vessels.

### Why that doesn't mean it clears alcohol

Alcohol isn't removed by the urea cycle. Your liver breaks alcohol down mainly with two enzymes: alcohol dehydrogenase turns it into acetaldehyde, and aldehyde dehydrogenase turns acetaldehyde into acetate, which is harmless. Citrulline isn't part of either step, and there's no good evidence that eating it speeds either one up. Ammonia isn't a meaningful cause of an ordinary hangover in a healthy person, so helping the body handle ammonia doesn't address what's making you feel bad. A healthy liver also already has plenty of capacity to run the urea cycle without extra citrulline from fruit.

So the word "detox" is doing a lot of work in those claims. Your liver doesn't need watermelon to process alcohol, and watermelon doesn't make it work faster.

### What the citrulline studies actually tested

Citrulline has a real research base, just not on hangovers:

- **Exercise and muscle soreness.** Citrulline and watermelon juice have been studied as sports supplements. One often-cited small study published in the *Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry* found that athletes who drank watermelon juice reported somewhat less muscle soreness after exercise. Results across the wider citrulline-and-exercise research are mixed.
- **Blood pressure and blood flow.** Because of the nitric oxide link, citrulline supplements have been studied for blood pressure and blood vessel function, with modest and inconsistent results.
- **Alcohol and the liver in animals.** A small number of studies in mice and rats have looked at whether citrulline supplements reduce liver damage from alcohol feeding. These are early findings in animals given controlled doses, not evidence about a person eating watermelon the morning after a party.

Two more caveats. First, the studies that found effects generally used concentrated citrulline supplements or large volumes of juice, and you'd need to eat a lot of watermelon flesh to match those doses. Second, none of them measured hangover symptoms. When people say "studies show citrulline helps hangovers," what they usually mean is that studies exist on citrulline, and the hangover part is a leap.

### Could the nitric oxide effect make a headache worse?

You'll occasionally see the opposite worry: since nitric oxide widens blood vessels, and some headache-triggering drugs work through nitric oxide, could watermelon worsen a hangover headache? There's no good evidence of that either. The amount of citrulline in a normal serving of watermelon is small compared with drug doses, and there's no reason for a social drinker to avoid watermelon on headache grounds. If you find it seems to bother you, simply skip it.

## Watermelon and Hydration

This is watermelon's real strength. Because it's around 92% water, a large bowl gives you a meaningful amount of fluid in a form that's often easier to get down than a big glass of water when you're queasy. Eating water-rich foods counts toward your daily fluid intake just like drinking does.

Alcohol makes you pee more because it blocks a hormone called vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. That's why you might wake up thirsty with a dry mouth. Replacing that lost fluid is reasonable and helps with thirst, dry mouth, and some of the lightheadedness.

There are limits, though:

- **It's a slow way to get a lot of fluid.** You'd need to eat about two cups of watermelon to match one standard glass of water. Use it alongside drinking, not instead of it.
- **It has almost no sodium.** Your body holds on to water better when it comes with some sodium. That's the reasoning behind oral rehydration solutions. If you're properly dried out after vomiting or diarrhea, plain watermelon isn't enough.
- **More water doesn't mean no hangover.** Rehydrating helps the thirsty, dried-out feeling but doesn't touch the inflammation and sleep loss.

For a step-by-step approach to fluids after a night out, see our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking).

## Watermelon Juice for a Hangover

Watermelon juice is popular in hangover lists, and it has some advantages: it's easy to drink, cold, and gets the fluid in faster than chewing through a bowl of cubes. The tradeoffs:

- **Less fiber, faster sugar.** Blending keeps more fiber than pressing, but either way the sugar hits your bloodstream faster than from whole fruit. A large glass of pressed juice can contain the sugar of several cups of fruit.
- **Store-bought versions vary.** Some bottled watermelon drinks have added sugar or are blends with cheaper juices. Check the label if you're watching sugar.
- **Same evidence gap.** Juice doesn't make the citrulline story any stronger.

A simple homemade version works well: blend two cups of cubed watermelon with a squeeze of lime and a small pinch of salt, then strain if you like it smooth. The salt isn't for flavor alone. It adds a little sodium, which plain watermelon lacks, turning it into something closer to a light homemade electrolyte drink. Keep the pinch small; you're aiming for "faintly salty," not seawater. Sipping it slowly is gentler on an unsettled stomach than gulping.

## Does Watermelon Help With Hangover Nausea?

For many people, yes, at least as a tolerable thing to eat. Cold, mild, water-rich foods are often the easiest to keep down when you feel sick, and watermelon fits that description well. Small amounts of sugar can also help if part of your shakiness or nausea comes from low blood sugar, which can happen after heavy drinking on an empty stomach.

Some tips if you're queasy:

- **Start small.** A few chilled cubes, then wait 15 to 20 minutes.
- **Eat it slowly.** Large amounts of cold fruit eaten fast can upset a sensitive stomach.
- **Follow it with something plain.** Toast, crackers, rice, or a banana give your stomach something more substantial.

If you're actively vomiting, hold off on food and focus on small sips of fluid until things settle. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers what to try and in what order.

## When Watermelon Can Make Things Worse

Watermelon is generally a safe food, but it isn't the best pick for everyone the morning after.

### Bloating, gas, and loose stools

Watermelon is high in fructose and also contains sugar alcohols and fermentable fibers. Monash University, which developed the low-FODMAP diet for irritable bowel syndrome, classes watermelon as high-FODMAP, meaning it contains carbohydrates that some people absorb poorly. In sensitive people, these pull water into the gut and get fermented by gut bacteria, which can cause gas, bloating, cramps, and diarrhea.

Alcohol already speeds up your gut and irritates its lining, which is why loose stools the next day are so common. Piling a large bowl of watermelon on top of that can make it worse if you're prone to fructose trouble or have IBS. If that's you, keep the portion small or pick a lower-FODMAP fruit such as a firm banana, oranges, or grapes. Our guide on [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) explains what's going on and what helps.

### Blood sugar

Watermelon has a high glycemic index, meaning its sugar is absorbed quickly, but a normal serving contains only a modest amount of sugar, so its overall effect on blood sugar is small. People with diabetes can usually fit a portion in, but should be aware that alcohol itself can drop blood sugar hours after drinking, especially in people taking insulin or certain diabetes medications. Watermelon is not a reliable fix for a low blood sugar episode; if you have diabetes and feel shaky, sweaty, or confused after drinking, check your blood sugar and follow your treatment plan.

### Spiked watermelon

Vodka-soaked watermelon is a classic party food, and it deserves a mention because it can cause the hangover you're now trying to treat. It's very hard to tell how much alcohol is in a slice, and because it tastes like fruit, people often eat far more than they would drink. If you're making or eating it, treat each few pieces as a drink and keep count.

## Should You Eat Watermelon Before Drinking?

Eating before drinking is one of the most useful things you can do, because food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream. But the kind of food matters. Meals with protein, fat, and fiber slow stomach emptying the most. Watermelon is almost all water and a little sugar, so it passes through quickly and does little to slow absorption on its own.

The better approach:

- **Eat a proper meal first,** such as something with eggs, chicken, fish, beans, rice, potatoes, or bread.
- **Add watermelon on the side** if you like it. It contributes some fluid, which doesn't hurt.
- **Don't treat a fruit plate as "lining your stomach."** It doesn't do the job a real meal does.

Some people also notice that a watery snack makes them need to pee more, which can be inconvenient on a night out. That's not harmful, just something to plan for.

## Watermelon While Drinking

Snacking on watermelon between drinks is a fine habit. It adds a bit of fluid and slows you down a little, which helps. It won't counteract the alcohol, though, and it's no substitute for alternating drinks with water. If you're in the sun, at a barbecue, or at a festival, the combination of heat, sweating, and alcohol dries you out faster than you'd expect. Watermelon plus water plus some salty food is a sensible pairing in that setting.

## Best Ways to Eat Watermelon When Hungover

Watermelon works best as one part of a recovery breakfast rather than the whole thing. A few combinations that make nutritional sense:

### Watermelon with a pinch of salt

The simplest upgrade. A light sprinkle of salt on chilled cubes adds some sodium and, for many people, makes the fruit taste sweeter. Some people add lime juice and a dusting of chili powder, a common way watermelon is served in Mexico.

### Watermelon and feta

Watermelon with crumbled feta, mint, and a little olive oil is a popular salad for good reason. The feta brings salt and protein, the oil adds fat, and the combination is more filling than fruit alone.

### Watermelon with eggs or toast

Have a few slices alongside eggs and toast. The eggs bring protein and some of the nutrients people associate with hangover recovery, and the toast gives steadier carbohydrate. Our guide on [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) explains what eggs can and can't do.

### Watermelon smoothie

Blend watermelon with plain yogurt or a scoop of protein powder, a banana, and ice. The yogurt or protein adds substance, and the banana adds some potassium and makes the texture creamier. Keep it simple if your stomach is unsettled.

### Watermelon "slushie"

Freeze watermelon cubes, then blend them with a splash of water, lime, and a tiny pinch of salt. Cold and easy to sip, it's a gentle way to get fluid in when even water seems unappealing.

## Watermelon vs Other Hangover Foods and Drinks

Here's how watermelon stacks up against other common choices. None of these cures a hangover; they differ in what they're good for.

| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Watermelon | Very hydrating, easy on nausea, light, pleasant | Almost no sodium, low in protein, can bloat sensitive stomachs |
| Plain water | Free, simple, the basis of rehydration | No sodium or sugar; can feel hard to get down |
| [Coconut water](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) | Fluid plus potassium | Low in sodium compared with rehydration drinks; can be pricey |
| Oral rehydration solution (like Pedialyte) | Balanced sodium and sugar designed to rehydrate | Taste; more than most people need after a mild night |
| Sports drinks | Some sodium and sugar, easy to find | Sugar content can be high; less sodium than rehydration solutions |
| [Bananas](/never-hungover/bananas-for-hangover) | Gentle on the stomach, some potassium, easy carbs | Little fluid, the potassium story is mostly a myth |
| [Orange juice](/never-hungover/orange-juice-for-hangover) | Fluid, vitamin C, sugar | Acidic, which can sting a sore stomach |
| Eggs and toast | Protein and steady carbs, filling | Not much fluid |

If your main problem is thirst and a dry mouth, watermelon is a good choice. If you've been sick or had diarrhea, an oral rehydration drink matters more. If you're starving and shaky, you need a real meal. For a broader look at what to eat, see our guide to the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover), and for drinks, our [electrolyte drinks comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared).

## Who Should Be Careful With Watermelon

Watermelon is safe for nearly everyone in normal amounts. A few groups should think twice about eating a lot of it:

- **People with IBS or fructose malabsorption.** As above, it's a high-FODMAP fruit that can trigger bloating and diarrhea.
- **People with diabetes.** Fine in sensible portions, but count it, and be aware that alcohol itself can cause low blood sugar later.
- **People with advanced kidney disease** who have been told to limit fluid or potassium. Watermelon is lower in potassium than many fruits, but large amounts still add up, and it adds fluid. Follow the limits your care team has given you.
- **Anyone with a melon allergy.** Melon allergies exist and are sometimes linked to ragweed pollen allergy. If your mouth itches or tingles when you eat it, stop.

## Citrulline Supplements and Watermelon Extracts

Because of the citrulline story, you'll find L-citrulline powders, watermelon extract capsules, and watermelon-flavored "recovery" products marketed in hangover circles. There is no good evidence that any of them prevent or treat hangovers. L-citrulline is generally considered well tolerated at typical supplement doses, but some people get stomach upset, and anyone taking blood pressure medication, nitrates, or erectile dysfunction drugs should check with a doctor or pharmacist first, since citrulline's effect on nitric oxide could add to those medicines' blood-pressure-lowering effect. In practice, if you like watermelon, eat watermelon; a supplement adds cost without adding a proven benefit for hangovers.

## A Realistic Hangover Morning (Where Watermelon Fits)

If you've woken up rough, this order tends to work better than any single food:

1. **Start with fluid.** A glass of water, or a bowl of chilled watermelon if water feels hard to face.
2. **Add some sodium if you've been sick.** An oral rehydration drink, a salty broth, or watermelon with a pinch of salt.
3. **Eat something substantial when you can.** Eggs, toast, oatmeal, rice, or soup. Watermelon on the side is fine.
4. **Treat specific symptoms carefully.** For a headache, a standard dose of a pain reliever with food may help, but read up first on the risks of mixing painkillers with alcohol, especially acetaminophen.
5. **Rest.** Sleep after drinking is poor quality, and making some of it up helps more than any food.
6. **Watch for warning signs.** If you're getting worse rather than better, or have any of the red flags in the box at the top, get medical help.

## Preventing the Next One

The most reliable way to avoid needing a recovery bowl of watermelon is the unglamorous one: drink less, drink slower, eat a real meal before you start, and alternate alcoholic drinks with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also use supplements. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on the brain's response to alcohol. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. It's promising, but there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers outright, and it doesn't replace food, water, or moderation. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically take it, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Pair it with a proper meal, plenty of water, and a bowl of watermelon in the morning if that's what you feel like.

## The Bottom Line

- Watermelon is a good food to eat when hungover, mainly because it's about 92% water and easy on a queasy stomach.
- It is not a cure. There is no good evidence that it shortens a hangover or helps your body clear alcohol faster.
- The citrulline "detox" claim is a stretch. Citrulline helps the liver handle ammonia, not alcohol, and its research is on exercise, blood flow, and animal liver studies rather than hangovers.
- Watermelon has almost no sodium, so pair it with salty food or a rehydration drink if you've been vomiting, sweating heavily, or had diarrhea.
- It's high in fructose, so a big bowl can worsen bloating or loose stools in sensitive people.
- Eating it before drinking is fine, but it doesn't slow alcohol absorption the way a meal with protein and fat does.
- If you can't keep fluids down, feel faint, or are getting worse, get medical help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is watermelon good for a hangover?**

Yes, as food and as a source of fluid, but not as a cure. Watermelon is about 92% water, easy to eat when you feel queasy, and gives you a little sugar for energy. There is no good evidence that it shortens or lessens a hangover on its own. Eat it with water and a proper meal for the best effect.

**Does the citrulline in watermelon help a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that it does. Citrulline helps your liver turn ammonia into urea and helps your body make nitric oxide, but it plays no part in breaking down alcohol or acetaldehyde. Research on citrulline has focused on exercise, blood pressure, and a few animal studies of alcohol-related liver damage, none of which measured hangover symptoms in people.

**Is watermelon juice good for a hangover?**

It's a pleasant, easy way to get fluid in, especially if you're struggling with plain water. It doesn't do more than whole watermelon, and pressed juice concentrates the sugar. Adding a small pinch of salt and a squeeze of lime gives it a little sodium, which plain watermelon lacks.

**Does watermelon hydrate you better than water?**

Not better, but it does count. Watermelon is mostly water, so eating it contributes to rehydration, and its small amount of sugar and potassium doesn't hurt. You'd need about two cups of watermelon to equal one glass of water, so use it alongside drinking. If you've lost a lot of fluid from vomiting or diarrhea, an oral rehydration solution with sodium is more effective.

**Should I eat watermelon before drinking?**

It's fine, but it isn't enough on its own. Food slows alcohol absorption mainly when it contains protein, fat, and fiber, and watermelon has very little of any of those. Eat a proper meal before drinking and treat watermelon as a side.

**Can watermelon upset your stomach after drinking?**

It can in some people. Watermelon is high in fructose and other fermentable carbohydrates, and Monash University classes it as high-FODMAP. If you have IBS or are sensitive to fruit sugars, a large portion can cause bloating, gas, or diarrhea, which alcohol already makes more likely. Stick to a small serving or choose a different fruit.

**Does watermelon help hangover nausea?**

It often helps as something tolerable to eat. Cold, mild, watery foods are easier to keep down when you feel sick, and the small amount of sugar can help if low blood sugar is part of the problem. Start with a few cubes and wait before eating more. If you're actively vomiting, focus on small sips of fluid first.

**Is spiked watermelon worse for a hangover?**

It can be, mainly because it's hard to tell how much alcohol you're eating. Vodka-soaked watermelon tastes like fruit, so people often have far more than they realize. Treat a few pieces as roughly one drink and keep count.
